startHere.why: The hosts’ ten core frameworks in one intimate sitting, touching almost every thread on this map.
The show’s most-linked episode: freedom as the route to prosperity, told through India’s economic history.
Why every act of government is an act of violence: the foundation Amit names for the show’s state thread.
Ajay demystifies finance through its history, a foundation that 15 later episodes link back to.
The show’s biggest question, why India is poor, with a sharp critique of development economics.
One of the show’s most popular episodes: a lifetime of thinking about education, with advice for parents and young people.
Ajay’s family-firms masterclass opens the firms thread; Amit says the show taught him how central firms are to growth.
Amit’s poker presentation shows the hosts at play while teaching expected value, luck and equanimity.
A primer on why and how to read, which Amit counts among the show’s best episodes.
The lighter side: seven stories that should be films, proof the hosts aren’t just dry people into ideas.

threads.name: What the state should do, and what it shouldn’t
threads.summary: Every act of government is ultimately backed by force, so when is it justified? Starting from the hosts’ first principles of the state and public choice theory, this thread tests that toolkit on vaccines, drugs, speech, financial privacy and digital public goods. You come away able to ask of any proposal: where is the coercion, and can the state actually pull it off?

path.why: The foundation: the state as a monopoly on violence, why every act carries a moral cost, and scope versus strength.
The decision framework: freedom as default, the four buckets of market failure, and the least intrusive fix.
Governments are people: how politicians, bureaucrats, special interests and voters follow incentives that work against citizens.
First test case: a vaccine is a private good, so when, if ever, may the state coerce?
Adds the second question, ‘Is it even possible?’, with four metrics for how hard an intervention is.
Alcohol, drugs, gambling, sex work: why criminalising acts without victims builds criminal firms and backfires.
Amit’s single bright line on speech, and why India’s weak state capacity calls for more free speech, not less.
Financial privacy as personal privacy: how surveillance crept in step by step, and why India’s KYC is the world’s worst.
Why UPI and Aadhaar aren’t true public goods, and what state monopoly and premature legibility cost us.
The hosts argue openly over whether the state should fund innovation at all, then agree on how.
James C Scott’s legibility, high modernism and metis: why brilliant planners keep producing monumental failures.
A glossary for the debate: what liberal, socialist, statist and libertarian really mean, plus the hosts’ own first principles.

threads.name: Building a state that works: rules, checks and legitimacy
threads.summary: The Indian state does many things badly; the hosts want it to do a few things well, starting with the rule of law. This thread asks what makes a state capable and safe from its own power: rules over discretion, separation of powers, decentralisation and legitimacy. It then tests those ideas on regulators, prosecutors, pensions and the GST, and on the populists who would tear them down.

path.why: The foundation: strong rules, not strong rulers. Credible commitment is the state’s real power and growth’s machinery.
Democracy as dispersion of power, not just voting: the fear test for arbitrary power, and how India got its checks.
Subsidiarity for a country too diverse for an all-powerful centre: a hundred states, many of them cities.
Winning elections isn’t legitimacy: four sources of a state’s right to rule, and what breaks without it.
Why a country isn’t a company: no bankruptcy, coercive power, rules versus deals, and very different time horizons.
Why policies don’t transplant: every institution makes ‘API calls’ to the rest of the economy, so fix foundations first.
How Indian regulators fused legislative, executive and judicial power into a ‘three-power monster’, and how to fix it.
Fixing investigation and prosecution so the party in power can’t harass opponents, when the process itself is the punishment.
Pensions as a test of state capability: Ajay’s insider account of building the NPS, and why reforms decay.
A great idea built badly: how the GST lost its way, and why economists, not tax collectors, should design taxes.
Building a state from scratch: you can’t rehearse coercive power in exile, and an institution’s DNA lives in its law.
The threat: the seven-point populist playbook, and why a fair election is more than a fair count.

threads.name: Firms: where prosperity is made
threads.summary: Ajay argues that India’s path from poor to rich runs through its firms. This thread follows how firms are owned and governed, how they grow, go global, learn and die well, and how the state helps or hobbles them. Amit says he hadn’t fully grasped how central firms are to growth until he made this show with Ajay.

path.why: The foundation: four designs, from the founder as ‘little deity’ to dispersed shareholders with a strong board.
How Indian firms went from regional satraps to national firms, and why a diverse India now demands adaptive ones.
Where firms get their capital: limited liability, joint-stock companies, and finance as the selector of which ideas grow.
Sun, Google and Amazon: audacious leaps of imagination, because execution is commoditised and imagination is scarce.
Going global: exporting is a market test, not a revenue game, and you can’t love exports yet hate multinationals.
Foreign firms as teachers: FDI’s ultimate prize is knowledge diffusion, and its unfairness to Indian firms is the point.
Creative destruction needs Shiva as well as Vishnu: bankruptcy frees people and capital trapped in zombie firms.
Wright’s Law is earned: why good firms learn from every unit made while bad firms just add volume.
Economic development is a story of firms: why the state should enable winners rather than pick them.
The flip side: firms are cells, the economy is the organism, and running a country like a company fails.
Why you should start one: an owner’s tender gaze, business as hypothesis testing, and a bias for action.
How to build it: obsess over customers, product over marketing, hire for values, optimise for truth-telling.

threads.name: Why India is poor, and how it gets rich
threads.summary: Why, even after adjusting for purchasing power, is India’s income per head a tenth of America’s? Starting from the hosts’ critique of development economics, this thread works through population, schools, farms, infrastructure, factories, jobs and taxes. You come away seeing development as the emergence of high-productivity firms rather than a big state building things.

path.why: The foundation: the 10x gap, why the Solow model failed, and the three pillars of development.
People are brains, not stomachs: why density drives prosperity and ‘population problems’ are governance problems.
Why more spending won’t fix schools: fund schooling not schools, and why schooling alone doesn’t cause development.
Coaching classes are the symptom; scarce education is a policy choice, so free the colleges to choose.
Farmers hobbled by land restrictions, MSPs and APMCs: the missing structural transformation out of subscale farms.
Infrastructure powered a services boom but not goods: find the binding constraint before you spend.
Three numbers show manufacturing is broken; Ajay lists twelve problems, five for the Union and seven for the states.
Don’t pick winners among sectors: modern manufacturing is high-skill, and services are now more tradable than goods.
Why picking winners fails, from subsidies to PLI, and what the state should do instead: enable winners.
India’s real problem is too few jobs: gig work as flexibility, a door for women and an urban NREGS.
Taxes should stay out of productive firms’ way; blocked input tax credit means India partly lost its VAT.
A worked example: Himalayan states and tourism, built as development for locals rather than scenery for visitors.
The capstone: Ajay’s last word on why India is poor, as labour and capital fail to mobilise into high-quality firms.

threads.name: The beauty of finance, and India’s long road to it
threads.summary: Finance looks forbidding from outside, but its history makes it click: it is the brain of the economy, deciding where capital goes. This thread starts there, then follows Ajay through the parts of Indian finance he worked on, from banking and inflation targeting to bankruptcy, pensions and crises, always tied back to first principles. It also covers what to do with your own savings.

path.why: The foundation: a guided history from early finance to banks and derivatives, showing why the whole edifice makes sense.
The map: banking, equity, currency controls, bankruptcy and monetary policy, and why India’s finance is still centrally planned.
Inflation as a tax on the poor, and Ajay’s inside story of how inflation targeting finally arrived.
From FERA to FEMA: why currency controls turn citizens into criminals, and floating rates absorb shocks.
The melting ice cube: why speed matters in bankruptcy, how the IBC was born, and how it fares in practice.
Why every defined-benefit pension blows up, and how the NPS fixed India’s, until the fire returned.
How financial surveillance crept in layer by layer, and why following the money doesn’t catch terrorists.
Your own money: why there’s no retirement number, plus the equity premium and global diversification as a free lunch.
Five types of financial crisis, why they will always happen, the toolkit to fight them, and Amit’s Austrian dissent.
The regulatory state’s failures, and the FSLRC blueprint: the fix lives in each regulator’s founding law.

threads.name: How India lost its freedom, and how reformers win it back
threads.summary: Why do free societies prosper, and why did independent India spend decades shackling its own people? This thread tells India’s economic history through the lens of freedom, from the planning era and the Emergency to 1991 and the quiet reformers who kept going after it. You come away understanding how change actually happens: slowly, through ideas and endurance, and rarely by seizing a crisis.

path.why: The foundation: freedom as consent is the route to prosperity, then India’s economic history from before Independence to today.
The silent second freedom movement, pitched as a web series: Narasimha Rao, Montek, KP Krishnan and other reformers.
How change really happens, in the state, society and yourself: the policy pipeline, quiet conversations and endurance.
The Soviet and Chinese contrast: economic, social and political freedom come as one package.
Was Gandhi a black swan, or was independence coming anyway? A debate on how much one person shapes history.
Mahalanobis, the Planning Commission and a bill to license sadhus: the high-modernist faith that experts should run society.
The Emergency up close: editors who crawled, a deadly sterilisation drive, and a woman jailed for friendship.
Nehru, Havel, Manmohan Singh: outsiders in politics, and the technocrat-plus-politician partnership that carried the 1991 reforms.
Why 1991 to 2011, India’s best era, was an openness story rather than a party story.
Against ‘never waste a crisis’: crises usually end badly, so fix the roof while the sun is shining.
The lens applied to now: after 50% US tariffs, domestic reform is trade policy and prosperity beats pride.
How the state turns citizens into subjects, and why India’s top-down ‘idea of India’ was bound to fail.

threads.name: Thinking like an economist: prices, incentives and the unseen
threads.summary: Why do well-meant policies so often hurt the people they aim to help? This thread builds the hosts’ core toolkit: the seen and the unseen, prices as carriers of information, and the fallacies our Stone Age brains fall for. It then puts the tools to work on farms, power grids, the rupee and gig work.

path.why: The two foundations: Bastiat’s seen and unseen, and Hayek’s insight that prices coordinate what no planner could know.
Friedman, Hayek, Coase and Bastiat: three papers and an essay that teach frames, not just conclusions.
Hazlitt’s one lesson, trace the longer effects on all groups, applied to public works, taxes, tariffs and rent control.
Zero-sum, composition, post hoc, chess pieces, open-ended: five traps our Stone Age brains fall into.
Price caps, rent control, minimum wages, MSPs and tariffs: what happens every time the state fiddles with prices.
Beliefs that make elites feel virtuous while hurting the poor, from socialism and inequality to banning victimless crimes.
The toolkit on a real crisis: storage isn’t hoarding, speculation is insurance, and APMC monopsonies squeeze farmers.
Prices to the rescue: flexible electricity prices bridge the gap between solar power at noon and demand at dusk.
The most important price of all, and why calling the rupee ‘strong’ or ‘weak’ is meaningless.
Steelmans the critics, then asks ‘better than what?’ to argue gig work means freedom and empowerment.
The capstone: the ten frameworks that shaped the hosts, from spontaneous order to the double thank-you moment.

threads.name: Trade, globalisation and the borders in our heads
threads.summary: Why is trade between strangers a double thank-you moment, and why do countries keep building walls anyway? This thread runs from the first principles and history of globalisation to Trump’s tariffs, the US-China tech war and India’s options. It ends with the borders, and the nationalism, we carry in our heads.

path.why: The 101: who is the state to stop a voluntary exchange, comparative advantage, and tariff myths busted.
Ajay’s three waves of globalisation, and why today’s ‘third globalization’ comes conditioned by economic statecraft.
From Smoot-Hawley and GATT to Trump’s tariffs: why the trading system stalled, and India’s opening.
The firm’s-eye view: internationalisation is more than exports, and exporting cleans up a toxic political economy.
Why India keeps fighting foreign investment, from ‘hot money’ fears to anti-foreigner reflexes, and why 2025 is its window.
The US-China tech war: extraterritorial export controls, the third globalization in action, and whether sanctions work.
A roadmap after 50% US tariffs: deep trade agreements with rules-based democracies, and domestic reform as trade policy.
The gravity model of human interaction, why borders hurt those who live on them, and South Asia’s missing trade.
Culture as khichdi: food, clothes and language have always crossed borders, and once here, they’re ours.
Nationalism is not patriotism: tribal instincts, imagined communities, and economic nationalism as protectionism wearing a flag.

threads.name: War, security and the changing face of conflict
threads.summary: You can’t understand the state without understanding war. These episodes treat Ukraine as a laboratory, then turn to India’s military, counterinsurgency, hybrid and economic warfare, and where drones and cheap technology are taking conflict. The recurring lesson: economies, brains and freedom win wars, not machismo.

path.why: The foundation: why a faraway war matters, why authoritarian militaries fail, and why economies win wars.
Starting from Perun’s analysis: a young country with an old army, and how to build a better one beside it.
Counterinsurgency is 20% military and 80% political: what India keeps getting wrong in Kashmir and Naxal areas.
War stories built for the screen: Churchill’s hardest call, the Doolittle Raid, and a comedian who wouldn’t leave Kiev.
War in the grey zone, hard to detect, attribute or answer, and why India is already a battlefield.
Economic warfare: does it beat real warfare? The hosts openly disagree over the US-China tech war.
Reading Russia’s wartime economy from space with Ajay’s nighttime-lights data, because strategic war is economic war.
The frontier: drones, Operation Spiderweb and Taiwan, and why small, cheap and civilian now beats exquisite platforms.

threads.name: How progress happens: talent, heretics and technology
threads.summary: Where do breakthroughs come from, and why do so many institutions smother them? This thread moves from how knowledge is made and spread, through clusters of talent and the outlaws who defied convention, to technologies from Unix to AI. You come away knowing which conditions let ideas flourish, and how easily knowledge can be lost.

path.why: The foundation: how knowledge is produced, diffused and used, and how journals and credentialism hollowed out the academy.
The O-ring theory of talent: why great work needs the right place and people, from the Challenger to Bollywood.
Newton as the last of the magicians: genius is expressed by historical conditions, and capitalism and ideas form one continuum.
CR Rao, Abraham Wald and survivorship bias: statistics as thinking, and excellence that comes from founders, not bureaucracies.
Ajay’s hero: the maverick comes as a package, extraordinary times let him in, and the mediocre push back.
Wollstonecraft, Semmelweis, Wegener, Karikó: pioneers reviled in their lifetimes, and why the conventional-minded attack them.
Sparked by Amit’s heart attack: heretics who rethought their fields, from heart catheters to cricket, and the gatekeepers who decide.
Bell Labs and the Unix philosophy: how a culture of eccentrics, frugality and freedom built the backbone of modern technology.
Silphium, Dhaka muslin, Fogbank: knowledge isn’t simply cumulative, and tacit skill dies without practice.
Ajay’s decades of writing papers distilled: a paper is a unit of knowledge, written for the reader, not a credential.
Breaking silos: what economists can learn from anthropologists and sociologists, and how a non-specialist should read papers.
Moore’s Law as an economic law, not a law of physics, and why humans are bad at exponential thinking.
Maps from Everest’s surveys to real-time pictures of the world: technology as an end run around low state capacity.
A technology with a bad name: nuclear is the safest energy, and authoritarianism, not physics, caused Chernobyl.
The AI debate: Ajay sees statistics and a tool for a master, while Amit rejects AI doom.
Fifteen humble predictions for 2050, from AI-generated entertainment and gene editing to robotic war and lab-grown meat.

threads.name: Know thyself: evolution, desire, faith and culture
threads.summary: What hardware did evolution give us, and what software has culture written on top of it? This thread runs from natural selection and sexuality to culture, religion and atheism, then to what genes, search data and dating apps reveal about us. Throughout, the hosts warn against deriving an ‘ought’ from an ‘is’: hardwiring is not destiny.

path.why: The foundation: natural selection as the ultimate spontaneous order, design without a designer, and the key to knowing yourself.
Evolution applied to desire: what revealed preferences show about men and women, and why hardwiring isn’t destiny.
The pilot’s big frame: culture as the operating system on our hardware, plus preference falsification and conformism’s four quadrants.
Culture is a khichdi: most ‘Indian’ food came from elsewhere, and cultural appropriation is incoherent.
Amit’s path to non-belief: atheism as an absence of belief, and which of religion’s four jobs reason can take over.
Not a name but a river: a history of Hinduism that resists simple stories, through colonialism, Hindutva and caste.
What genetic data says about our mixed prehistory and caste endogamy, and what phone battery life reveals about character.
Search data, dating apps and innovative surveys reveal what we really want, from the Tinder Gini to the sex recession.
Human nature meets technology: relationships remapped, marriage unbundled, and reproduction moving inside machines by 2050.

threads.name: Stories, art and the creator’s craft
threads.summary: Amit believes stories illuminate the world, and these episodes show the hosts are not just dry people who are into ideas. This thread gathers their stories that should be films, the plots beneath all stories, how form and constraint shape art, and Amit’s lessons on podcasting and building a body of work. You come away with a storyteller’s eye and a creator’s playbook.

path.why: Where it began: a nonviolent ‘warrior’ tribe, the fat frogs of Tatsinskaya, and a child widow who remade her world.
Grand canvas, intimate story: a couple who hear the world differently, and VP Menon stitching together independent India.
Fiction about IIT aspirants and vloggers alongside true stories: missing plutonium on Nanda Devi and a Delhi in churn.
A thief of electricity bills, two Sikhs defending a bridge, a child in the mail, and Chekhov’s gun.
Christopher Booker’s seven basic plots: the skeletons under every story, and why structure isn’t a constraint.
Springsteen as literature: write what’s around you, the specific becomes universal, and never play cover versions of yourself.
Joni Mitchell, Frida Kahlo, Dr Seuss and Fosbury: how constraints, imposed or chosen, become a creative force.
Velázquez to Miró: why Spain’s masters did their most powerful work in old age, when thehraav met mastery.
A golden age for creators: they now own the means of production, so play the long game.
Songs, albums and films took their shape from old storage limits; creators can now find true fans instead of scale.
Amit’s podcasting masterclass: write for the ear, take guests out of autocomplete mode, and be loved by a few.
Eight crises of the Indian media, from relevance to attention, and why the future lies in monetising community, not ads.
The capstone: stock and flow, authenticity, and the long game, from a show that never missed a week.

threads.name: Private passions: games, sport, books and art
threads.summary: In the finale, Amit says the show fused public purpose with private passion. These are the passion episodes, each built from a lifetime of loving something: poker, cricket, chess, cycling, hiking, reading, music, painting and Unix. Each doubles as a lesson in decisions, luck, character or craft.

path.why: The foundation: Amit’s poker primer on expected value, tilt and position, and why poker leads to equanimity.
Expected value and opportunity cost applied to cricket: how T20 changed the game, and why to judge decisions, not outcomes.
From 1886 to Gukesh: world championships, AlphaZero, and why computers diversified chess instead of flattening it.
Gukesh, Arjun and Magnus as life lessons: the world isn’t static, and power corrodes. Amit’s underrated favourite.
Slipstream makes cycling a team sport: strategy, cooperate-then-defect tactics, and how doping was cleaned up.
Ajay’s lifelong love: why city-dwelling monkeys need nature, how to start hiking safely, and character under stress.
Why read, how to build the habit, how to read a book: a primer Amit counts among the show’s best.
What Springsteen means to Ajay personally, and what Amit admires in a rock star whose work is literature.
Amit’s holiday education in Spanish painting, and the late mastery of Velázquez, Goya, Picasso and Miró.
Ajay’s love of Unix, with a screencast: small tools, plain text, pipes, and good file names as a superpower.

threads.name: Life lessons: habits, choices and a life well spent
threads.summary: How do you get things done, make good choices under uncertainty and spend your days well? This thread gathers the hosts’ practical wisdom on productivity, serendipity, decluttering, health, money and meaning, with the AMA and Good Gyan episodes along the way. It ends with the frameworks that shaped them both.

path.why: The foundation: kaator re bhaaji, just cut the vegetables. Habits are the whole game, and you suck at the start.
Habits applied to health: Amit’s diabetes reversal through keto, fasting and a glucose monitor, and the sugar lobby’s dangerous consensus.
Serendipity as excellence times exposure: put yourself out there, but don’t demand the lollipop before doing the work.
Don’t let incentives freeze you into one version of yourself; longer lives need more than one persona.
The pilot: uncles and anti-uncles, why the aggressively conventional-minded hold us back, and books as extra lives.
The things you own end up owning you: decluttering stuff, preoccupations and toxic people, while embracing productive mess.
Twitter’s best minds, curated: attach confidence to every belief, and learn a field in the order it developed.
More gyan: thin versus thick desires, imperfectionism done right, and why there’s no ‘making it’.
Mixtapes, handwritten letters, address books: what lost objects say about effort, scarcity and ‘the last time you did X’.
Why the retirement number is the wrong question: process over destination, calm over control, and women owning their finances.
Rapid verdicts and lively disagreements: failure is underrated, frugality buys freedom, and solitude isn’t loneliness.
The 50th-episode AMA: your hours build your future self, pick one thing and find a master, and denormalise three behaviours.
The 100th-episode AMA: life as managing luck, money as blood and time as the real scarcity, and rejecting victimhood.
The intimate capstone: play to play, life is not a spectator sport, and give unconditionally.
